closing_note.summary: A 55-year-old man presents with two years of persistent sub-nephrotic proteinuria (1,259 mg/24h), mild CKD (eGFR 61.6), and a biochemical pattern of proximal tubular dysfunction: markedly elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin and alpha-1-microglobulin, glycosuria with alkaline urine pH, and an electrolyte profile (phosphate 1.36, potassium 3.7, bicarbonate 22.7, uric acid 300 µmol/L) consistent with partial Fanconi syndrome. Serum albumin is preserved, arguing against a nephrotic glomerulopathy. Serum immunofixation demonstrates a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak with free kappa 427.5 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 50.47. This paraprotein burden, combined with the tubular injury pattern, makes light chain proximal tubulopathy the leading working diagnosis. Three prioritised explanations: Light chain proximal tubulopathy – supported by the kappa-restricted paraprotein, tubular proteinuria, and partial Fanconi pattern. Drug or toxin-induced Fanconi syndrome – cannot be excluded as exposure and medication records are unavailable at this decision point. Other paraprotein-related renal disease (e.g. cast nephropathy or amyloidosis) – less likely given the tubular-predominant pattern and sub-nephrotic proteinuria, but not excluded without biopsy. Next discriminating steps: renal biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to confirm light chain crystal or granular inclusions; haematological staging (bone marrow, skeletal survey) to classify the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia; and documentation of medication and occupational history to exclude alternative Fanconi causes.

state.final_answer:
Clinical Problem
A 55-year-old man presents with two years of persistent sub-nephrotic proteinuria (1,259 mg/24 h), mildly reduced eGFR (61.6 mL/min/1.73 m²), and normal serum albumin. Urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L) are markedly elevated alongside glycosuria and alkaline urine pH, indicating proximal tubular dysfunction. Serum immunofixation reveals a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak with free kappa 427.5 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 50.47.

Prioritised Explanations
Light chain proximal tubulopathy: The combination of a significant kappa paraprotein and a tubular-pattern proteinuria with glycosuria is the most coherent unifying diagnosis. Uncertainty remains because renal biopsy is withheld, so the pathological subtype is unconfirmed.
Alternative Fanconi syndrome causes: Drug, toxin, or autoimmune aetiologies cannot be excluded; medication and exposure histories are unavailable at this decision point.
Other paraprotein-related kidney disease: Cast nephropathy or amyloidosis are less consistent with the tubular marker pattern but cannot be excluded without tissue.

Next Information/Actions
Renal biopsy with Congo red and light-chain immunostaining is the key discriminating investigation. Haematological staging (marrow, skeletal survey) is needed to classify the plasma cell disorder. Urine immunofixation and a medication/exposure history should be obtained. Serial creatinine monitoring is warranted given the absence of a pretreatment trajectory.
